## What can we do reduce atmospheric CO~2~?

-   Decrease emissions of fossil fuels
-   Increase removals from the atmosphere
-   What removes CO~2~ from the atmosphere?

## Concepts in the global carbon budget

-   ⚫️ Stocks: where you can find carbon stored
-   ⬆️ Fluxes: the transfer of carbon between stocks
-   Units are Gigatons of C / year (Giga = 10\^9, 1 ton = 1000 grams)
-   1 Gt = 1,000,000,000 water bottles

## Global Carbon Budget

![](assignment/img/carbon-budget-2025.png){fig-align="center" fig-alt="diagram of 2022 global carbon budget"}

~https://doi.org/10.5194/essd-2025-659~

## Role of vegetation in global carbon budget

-   9.8 Gt/yr emissions to atmospheric CO~2~
-   Atmospheric CO~2~ only goes up by 5.6 (Gt/yr) = 57% (half the warming!)
-   25% of emissions are absorbed by terrestrial ecosystems

## Vegetation carbon is important

-   Increasing carbon on land (e.g., forests) decreases carbon in the atmosphere
-   Decreasing carbon in the atmosphere, decreasing global temperatures (or prevents more warming)
-   Can we manage the land to increase the amount of carbon in ecosystems?
-   Basis for carbon markets - you pay for my extra ecosystem carbon to offset your fossil fuel emissions)

::: aside
https://www.neonscience.org/field-sites/explore-field-sites
:::

## NEON Woody Carbon

-   Each site has a set of plots (either "tower" or "distributed")
-   Each tree is mapped (species)
-   Each year, each tree is measured: status (live or dead) and diameter

![](assignment/img/plot_design.png){fig-align="center" fig-alt="diagram of NEON plot design"}

## NEON Woody Carbon

-   Diameter can be converted to biomass using "allometric" relationships
-   Biomass can be converted to carbon (carbon = biomass x 0.5)
-   Allometric relationships are from Jenkin et al. (2004)

![](assignment/img/allometrics_plot.png){fig-align="center" fig-alt="graph of allometric relationship"}

## NEON Woody Carbon

-   Carbon for individual trees is summed within a plot to determine the plot carbon each year
-   The summed carbon is divided by the area (m\^2) of the plot to standardize across plots of different size
-   All plots within a site averaged to get a site-level carbon for each year.

![](assignment/img/plot_design.png){fig-align="center" fig-alt="diagram of NEON site design"}

## What is a database?

-   A structured, persistence storage of data
-   Relational (strict standards) vs Non-relational (more flexible)
-   We focus on relational databases here

## Database vs. CSV

-   A CSV is like a dataframe (table) where all columns need to have same number of rows
-   Databases can have multiple tables
-   Tables can have different numbers of rows
-   Database has data storage and access efficiency

## What is a relationship database?

-   Data in tables with rows and columns
-   Tables connect to one another through keys
    -   Primary (ids within a table) - one per table
    -   Foreign (reference ids in another table) - can have multiple per table

## You have the skills to work with databases!

-   Filter, Select, Group By, Summarize
-   Develop skills in joins within this module

## SQL is the databse language

-   SQL (Structured Query Language)
-   Tidyverse helps translate functions in SQL language
-   We focus on tidyverse approach but know that SQL is under the hood

```         
species <- tbl(con, "species") |>
  filter(genus == "Calamospiza") |> 
  select(taxa)
```

is actually

```         
"SELECT taxa FROM species WHERE genus == 'Calamospiza'"
```

in SQL

## "Brand" of database

-   Common types of relationship databases are PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, duckDB
-   We use duckDB in this class
-   Concepts and code access are largely the same with details different

## Accessing database

First connect to database

```         
library(DBI)
con <- dbConnect(duckdb::duckdb(), "rat_data.db")
```

extract data

```         
species <- tbl(con, "species") |>
  filter(genus == "Calamospiza") |> 
  select(taxa) |> 
  collect()
```

close database

```         
dbDisconnect(con)
```

## Building databases

-   Create database (or open existing)
-   Add tables
-   Be sure that tables have keys that connect them!
-   Be sure to append when adding data to existing database

## Keys are critical for joining tables with a database

-   Joins are used to combine tables
-   Pulling data from one table into another
-   Using one table to filter another table

## Mutating joins

- Never lose information from the left (or right) table so fills with NA
- Mutate join because add columns
- `left_join`: Keep all rows in the left side table (e.g., `df1` in `left_join(df1, df2)`)
- `right_join`: Keep all rows in the right side table (e.g., `df2` in `right_join(df1, df2)`) 
- `inner_join`: Keep all rows in both tables
- `full_join`: Keep all rows in either table

## Filtering joins

- Use information in one table to reduce the number of rows in another table
- Does not add columns to the left side.
- `semi_join`: keep rows in left side table with match in right table 
- `anti_join`: keeps rows in left side table without match in right table

## Defining keys

- tidyverse will try to detect the keys by looking at columns with the same names
- Better to specify the keys used to join tables
- While `left_join(df1, df2)` works, `left_join(df1, df2, by = c("site_id")` is better
- `by` allows you to join using columns with different names: `left_join(df1, df2, by = c("site_id" = "siteID")`
